engagement.justification: Prompt asks for material-conditional/modus-tollens reasoning about weather and planning, but the response is an unrelated essay on why withholding knowledge is sometimes wise.

coherence.justification: Three numbered reasons flow readably, though a few sentences ('If everyone knows how to do something bad without anyone ever doing it') garble and it ends mid-thought.

substance.justification: Offers several distinct reasons (idea-theft, safety, time-cost) but only enumerates them without pushing any into a real argument.

engagement.justification: Prompt names material-conditional/paradoxical inductive reasoning; response instead lays out the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge, only tangentially touching the inductive 'good reason' angle.

coherence.justification: The belief/truth/justification thread is mostly consistent though it shuffles the three conditions awkwardly and cuts off mid-sentence.

substance.justification: Develops the luck-vs-knowledge distinction and the modal 'would work even if you changed the situation' reliability point, real epistemological work.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for a predictive anomaly analogy in mechanical/repair; response is a generic good-reason-vs-bad-reason essay with no analogy or mechanical anomaly.

substance.justification: Names criteria for good reasons (fit, prior observation, repeatability) but treats them as a checklist without developing the predictive case.

engagement.justification: Gestures at the abstraction/causation theme the prompt implies but is too fragmentary to genuinely engage an epistemology question.

coherence.justification: Largely a run-on of half-formed clauses ('there is no way to think a thing we do not see works the same make') that does not hold together.

substance.justification: Barely reaches the correlation-isn't-causation idea but never develops it; mostly broken phrasing.

engagement.justification: Touches the correlation/causation idea loosely but ignores the legal cross-jurisdictional anomaly-analogy framing entirely.

coherence.justification: Short but internally consistent: states that co-occurrence without examining the connection doesn't establish causation.

substance.justification: Correctly identifies the correlation-causation distinction but is a one-line truism with no development.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for an argumentative anomaly analogy in epistemology, but the response is a veil-of-ignorance / original-position political-philosophy essay.

coherence.justification: The behind-the-wall thought experiment is developed consistently, though pronoun slips ('i must imagine that you are behind a wall') are sloppy and it trails off.

substance.justification: Genuinely reconstructs the original-position argument and ties impartiality to protecting the least-advantaged, real reasoning.

engagement.justification: Prompt wants an argumentative anomaly analogy in philosophy of mind; response instead explains logical validity/counterexample testing, off the named topic.

substance.justification: The counterexample method for testing entailment is a real idea, but the bungled example undercuts the work it does.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for indicative-conditional/modus-tollens reasoning in a criminal-law domain; response is a universalizability/contractualist ethics essay unrelated to that.

substance.justification: Develops a contractualist test and connects it to fairness and the veto of the disadvantaged, more than restatement.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for an explanatory abstraction analogy in physics; response is about why cooperative groups/promises hold together or break, no physics or stated analogy.

substance.justification: Identifies genuine factors in cooperation stability (fair payoffs, common knowledge, communication, defection incentives), real analysis.

engagement.justification: Vaguely about choosing between two bad options but ignores the indicative-conditional/modus-ponens weather-planning framing.

coherence.justification: The 'pick the middle of two bad ways' idea is graspable but the phrasing is clumsy and self-tangled ('stay away from the worst parts of either way but stay away from both').

substance.justification: Points at a real golden-mean/lesser-evil heuristic but only sketches it without development.

engagement.justification: Prompt names indicative-conditional/paradoxical perceptual reasoning; response argues that repeated kind acts make you kind, only loosely a conditional and off the perceptual topic.

coherence.justification: The habituation-into-virtue argument is consistent, though it opens with a stray 'one way that says if a person does a thing then that person is good' that doesn't fully resolve.

substance.justification: Traces a real mechanism (action -> self-perception change -> reinforced disposition), an Aristotelian habituation point with actual content.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for indicative-conditional/modus-tollens experimental reasoning; response is an essay on overconfidence and cognitive shortcuts, off-form and off-domain.

coherence.justification: The overconfidence argument is consistent and well-ordered across its enumerated points with no contradictions.

substance.justification: Explains overconfidence via cognitive economy and the cost of acting on false certainty, identifying what's at stake rather than restating.

engagement.justification: Prompt names material-conditional/modus-ponens deontological reasoning; response instead surveys consequentialism vs deontology vs virtue ethics, touching deontology only as one option.

substance.justification: Draws genuine distinctions between outcome-based, rule-based, and character-based ethics with apt illustrations, real conceptual work.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for a literal-similarity analogy in metaphysics; response critiques naive hedonic accounting, no analogy and off the metaphysics topic.

substance.justification: Raises real objections to utilitarian accounting (weighting, temporal effects, cascading consequences), genuine reasoning despite rough patches.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for probabilistic-conditional/affirming-consequent reasoning about social causation; response (after a 'when when when' artifact) is the withholding-knowledge essay again, unrelated.

substance.justification: Lists distinct considerations (idea appropriation, cognitive load, exclusivity) but enumerates rather than develops them.

engagement.justification: Glances at an abstraction/causation question but never engages the literary-allegory analogy the prompt names.

coherence.justification: Two short conditional-style questions are individually readable but disconnected and never resolved into a claim.

substance.justification: Only poses the screening-off / counterfactual-cause question without developing any answer.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for an explanatory anomaly analogy in metaphor; response is a justified-true-belief essay with no metaphor or anomaly addressed.

engagement.justification: Prompt names strict-conditional/affirming-consequent perceptual reasoning; response (after 'when when' artifact) argues rule-following ethics is insufficient, off-form and off-topic.

substance.justification: Makes a real point that codified rules underdetermine right action and that character fills the gap, genuine moral reasoning.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for a literal-similarity analogy in philosophy of mind; response is a belief-vs-knowledge essay, off the named topic and form.

substance.justification: Builds toward the JTB account, distinguishing true belief from knowledge via a reliable reason 'tied to how the world really is.'

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for a proper analogy in epistemology; response is an ethics-of-partiality essay about owing more to close relations, with no epistemology or explicit analogy.

engagement.justification: Prompt asks for a proper analogy in cooking/craft; response is a good-reason-vs-bad-reason epistemology essay with no analogy and no cooking content.

engagement.justification: Prompt names indicative-conditional/modus-ponens predicate reasoning; response is a general essay on what makes a thought's justification strong, only loosely a conditional.

substance.justification: Develops real epistemic criteria (observable grounding, ruling out alternative explanations, robustness under small changes, confirmation bias).
